newsitem.title: ITALY: Worldwatch body says population is key to hunger.
newsitem.headline: Worldwatch body says population is key to hunger.

text.p: An independent environmental research body said on Tuesday that the most important document a U.N.-sponsored World Food Summit could issue this week would need to contain just one word: "Help".

"The one thing that I would like to see from the conference is a letter from FAO Director General Jacques Diouf to his counterpart at the United Nations Population Fund," Worldwatch president Lester Brown told a news briefing.
"It could be a very short letter. In fact it need have only one word in it: Help."

Brown, in a view opposed by Pope John Paul who opens the summit on Wednesday, said the key to world food security for the next generation depended upon family planning and quickly curbing population growth.

The five-day summit, organised by the Rome-based United Nations Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO), will pledge to halve the 840 million people in the world suffering chronic hunger or malnutrition by 2015.
A formal declaration and plan of action have already been finalised for the five-day summit which FAO says will bring together around 100 heads of state and government.

While FAO was relatively optimistic about the world's ability to feed its ever expanding population, Worldwatch experts painted the gloomier picture of a planet entering a new era in which food scarcity was the defining issue.
Brown said the good news was that the rate of world population growth had been dropping for 20 years, from a rate of two percent in 1970 to 1.5 percent today.
The bad news was that the figure still represented 90 million more mouths to be fed every year.
"There has been more population growth in the world since 1950 than during the previous four million years since the day when we first stood upright," Brown declared.
"We must ask whether there is any moral foundation for couples having more than two children -- the replacement level. This is becoming increasingly an issue."
The rise in population, particularly in Asia, was coupled with increased affluence in the Far East which had put greater strains on water resources and agricultural land.
The populations of the emerging Asian nations were increasingly consuming costlier foods such as pork, milk and beer that required large amounts of grain to produce.

Brown said that China alone had gone from being a net exporter of grain in 1994 to the second largest importer in the world after Japan. At the same time the country was losing cropland and water at a record rate to factories.
Global warming -- with the 11 warmest years since records began in the mid-19th century occurring since 1979 -- raised the very real risk of crop failure and market chaos.

"In 1988 we had record heat in the United States combined with drought. It reduced the U.S. grain harvest below consumption for the first time in history. If 1988 happened again, there will be chaos on grain markets," said Brown.

Asked whether Worldwatch had a particular message for the Pope and the Roman Catholic Church, which fiercely opposes contraception, Brown related that he had once been awarded an honorary degree by the university of Pisa.
"I have two things in common with Galileo," said Brown, referring to the Italian medieval astronomer who incurred Papal wrath with his theories about gravity and the universe.
"One is that we both have degrees from Pisa. The other is that the Pope did not like us. If you have any advice on how to alter that I'd be very willing to hear it."
